Architecture

Source: vignettes/articles/architecture.Rmd
architecture.Rmd

sasonr treats SAS as the only source language and R as the execution engine. Nothing is translated “once and handed over”: the SAS program is parsed and executed every time, and the generated R code can be inspected.

SAS program text
   │
   ▼
Macro processor ──────────────── macro symbol tables, macro definitions (session)
   │  expands %LET, %IF, %DO, &x into SAS text; yields one complete step at
   │  a time. After the step runs, CALL SYMPUT(X) and SQL INTO: values are
   │  written back before expansion continues (expansion and execution
   │  interleave).
   ▼
Lexer: text → token table (line, column, kind; comments and blanks kept,
   │   so the tokens give the source back exactly)
   ▼
Parser: recursive descent for statements, Pratt parser for expressions
   │   (SAS operator precedence: comparison chains, IN, MIN/MAX, ...)
   ▼
AST: one tree per step (DATA, PROC SQL, PROC MEANS, ...), kept as written
   ├──► sas_check(): rules that list every unsupported feature before
   │    anything runs
   ▼
Analysis: types and lengths, readers (SET / MERGE / INPUT), BY, arrays
   ▼
Intermediate representation: declarations in slots (KEEP, LENGTH, RETAIN,
   │   BY, ...), executable statements as a control-flow graph
   ▼
Data-flow facts: which level can run this step?
   ├─ L1 / L2: dplyr pipelines (whole columns, BY groups, accumulators, LAG)
   └─ L3     : an explicit row loop (PDV, implicit OUTPUT, RETAIN)
   ▼
Code generation: R calls built with rlang; SAS functions become sas_f_*()
   │   PROC SQL → own SQL parser, DuckDB for joins and grouping
   │   other procedures → R implementations
   ▼
Engine: evaluates the step in its environment with the run-time helpers
   │   (fixed-length character storage, missing values, NOTEs, _ERROR_)
   ▼
Session: WORK data sets, options, titles, formats (carry over between steps)
   ▼
Output: log events      → the log (plain, coloured, HTML)
        ODS tables      → the listing, the HTML document, ODS OUTPUT data sets

DATA step compilation levels

What matters is the result of each step, not a replica of the program data vector, so each step is compiled to the fastest form that is provably equivalent to row-by-row execution:

Level Used when Generated code
L1 no cross-row state dplyr::mutate(), filter(), select()
L2 recognised patterns: BY groups with FIRST./LAST., RETAIN accumulators, baseline carry-forward, unconditional LAG grouped vectorised code
L3 anything else (conditional LAG, OUTPUT to several data sets, DO loops creating rows, …) an explicit row loop that follows the DATA step execution rules

The level is decided by data-flow facts on the control-flow graph. If a vectorised step meets a condition that needs row-by-row diagnostics (for example invalid data that sets _ERROR_), it is re-run as L3.

The session

Everything a SAS program can change lives in one session object (SasSession, an R6 class), never in package-level variables:

Component Contents
WORK data sets (tibbles), their metadata (types, lengths, formats, labels), PROC SQL views, _LAST_
Format catalog user formats and informats from PROC FORMAT
Macro global symbol table, local frames, macro definitions, automatic macro variables (SYSCC, SYSERR, SQLOBS, …)
Options LINESIZE, NOTES, SYNTAXCHECK, the listing layout (CENTER, DATE, NUMBER, PAGESIZE, FORMDLIM); options whose only implemented value is the SAS default (YEARCUTOFF=1940, ERRORS=20, MISSING=.) are not stored, other values fail loud
Titles, filerefs TITLE lines, FILENAME assignments
SQL back end the DuckDB connection, opened on first use and closed with the session
Sinks the cumulative log and listing of all submissions
Diagnostics compile-time NOTEs of the step being translated; run-time state of the step being run (_ERROR_ flag, data-error NOTEs, missing-value and math-error counters, observations read, PRXPARSE ids)

sas_run(code) creates a throw-away session; sas_session() creates one that several sas_run(code, session = s) calls share, one submission after another (each submission still starts outside syntax-check mode). sas_work(), sas_meta(), sas_macro_vars(), sas_log() and sas_listing() read a session.

The generated step code does not take the session as an argument. The engine binds the session for the duration of a submission and restores the previous binding on exit; the run-time helpers that generated code calls (sas_err_sync(), sas_put_line(), the functions and formats) read the bound session. Two sessions used alternately therefore never see each other’s state, and a sas_run() nested inside a running step gets its own session without disturbing the outer one; a nested submission to the same session is refused (it would rebind the running submission’s log and macro executor).

The listing has the layout of NOCENTER NODATE NONUMBER FORMDLIM=' ' PAGESIZE=MAX. A procedure that writes output while CENTER, DATE or NUMBER is set, while FORMDLIM= is not a blank (from the second page on), or with more lines than fit on one page of a finite PAGESIZE= fails loud.

Semantics across submissions

This state does not carry over from one submission to the next:

State Behaviour
Syntax-check mode after an ERROR reset at the start of each submission
PRXPARSE ids numbered from 1 in each submission
Log line numbers start at 1 in each submission
PROC SQL without QUIT; closed at the end of the submission
PROC SQL options (NUMBER, NOPRINT, …) reset with each submission

Function-layer calls made outside any run (sas_f_round() in your own code) have no hidden state: there is no default session. Their data-error NOTEs are discarded, they see no user formats and no filerefs, use LINESIZE=132 (or their .ls argument), and PRXPARSE ids need an explicit session (sas_f_prxparse(re, session = s)).

Parsed programs, translations and results are plain S3 values; the function, format and procedure-option registries are built once at load time and are never changed by a run.

Why not keyword mapping or regular expressions

A simpler design would tokenise the program and map each keyword to an R function. sasonr does map SAS functions to sas_f_*() at the end, but the layers in between are needed because the meaning of SAS code is rarely local to one keyword:

  • Context decides the statement. IF x; is a subsetting IF and IF x THEN a condition; = assigns or compares; PUT is a statement or a function; set, if and end can be variable names; a <= b in (0, 5) is a <= (b in (0, 5)). This needs a grammar, not a keyword table.
  • A DATA step is compiled before it runs. Types and lengths come from the first appearance of a variable, LENGTH, RETAIN and the data sets read; the program data vector exists before the first observation. A statement-by- statement mapping does not know the length of a variable when it meets it.
  • Many rules are implicit. Variables read by SET are retained, every iteration ends with an implicit OUTPUT, and in a match-merge the variables of a data set that has run out of rows in a BY group keep their last value. None of this is written in any statement; the intermediate representation holds it for the whole step.
  • Vectorisation needs the whole step. Only after the data-flow analysis shows that no value crosses rows can a step run as whole-column dplyr code; a mapping per statement can only produce a row loop.
  • Macros rewrite the program. What %IF &n > 0 %THEN ... generates is known only after an earlier step has set n with CALL SYMPUT, so macro expansion and execution have to interleave.
  • The log needs positions and structure. NOTEs give (Line):(Column) places taken from the tokens; line wrapping and syntax-check mode after an ERROR depend on the step structure.
  • Unsupported features are found before anything runs, and the same intermediate representation feeds the executed code, sas_translate() and the scripts of sas_script().

SAS syntax is not a regular language either (nested DO/END blocks, nested parentheses, operator precedence, macro expansion), so regex-based translation reaches a ceiling quickly; sasonr is fully deterministic.

Fail loud

Every statement, option, function and procedure is either implemented or rejected with a sasonr_unsupported condition that names the feature and the SAS line. Silent approximation is treated as a bug.
